title: Why a Dead Pinecone Still Moves When It Gets Wet | Why It Happens #5

hook_candidates.text: This pinecone is dead. So why is it moving?
Drop water on this cone. Watch it shut by itself.
This cone is eleven million years old. It still moves.
hook_candidates.note: true only for the fossil cones, and spends the climax in the hook

hook_candidates.text: You've seen pinecones closed after rain. Nothing alive closed them.
Watch this gap. A dead cone is about to close it.

parts.text: and every scale has to swing shut.
The bottom one stretches when wet,
opening the cone so wind can take the seeds.
Fossil cones over eleven million years old

sources: Cones close in wet conditions and open in dry conditions; the scale movement is passive and needs no metabolic energy: University of Freiburg press release on Poppinga et al. 2017, https://www.bio.uni-freiburg.de/news/20170111-speck-en ; Poppinga S. et al., 'Hygroscopic motions of fossil conifer cones', Scientific Reports 7, 40302 (2017), https://www.nature.com/articles/srep40302 .

'Dead': the scale tissue that does the moving (sclereids and sclerenchyma fibres) is dead at maturity, and the motion is purely passive swelling and shrinking (Poppinga et al. 2017; Dawson, Vincent & Rocca, 'How pine cones open', Nature 390, 668 (1997), https://www.nature.com/articles/37745 ).

Two layers: a highly swellable lower sclereid layer (cells about 20% longer when wet) under a much less swellable upper layer of sclerenchyma strands; the lower layer swelling bends the scale up and closes the cone, and drying pulls it down and opens it (Poppinga et al. 2017 introduction; Freiburg 2022 press release, https://www.bio.uni-freiburg.de/news/20220531-speck-en ). Freiburg 2022 (Advanced Science) shows the real tissue is more complex, with several swelling layers; the video labels its two-layer picture 'SIMPLIFIED MODEL'.

One layer alone does not bend: a uniformly swelling strip just gets longer; bending needs two layers that swell by different amounts (bilayer principle, Reyssat & Mahadevan, 'Hygromorphs: from pine cones to biomimetic bilayers', J. R. Soc. Interface 6, 951 (2009)). Shown as a labelled model.

Seeds are released when it is dry and they can be carried far by wind; under wet conditions, unfavourable for wind dispersal, the cone stays closed (Freiburg 2022 press release; Poppinga et al. 2017).

Fossil cones from the middle Miocene, about 16.5 to 11.5 million years old, and from the Eemian (126,000-113,000 years) still open and close their scales with moisture (Poppinga et al. 2017; Freiburg 2017 press release). Script says 'over eleven million years old', true for the Miocene cones.
